hints: Focus on solubility patterns for Group 2 compounds, carbonates and hydroxides are usually insoluble but chlorides and nitrates are soluble.
Work out the first step for both metals, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ with carbonate ions both give white carbonate precipitates.
Follow what excess acid does to a carbonate and what excess alkali does to the resulting chloride, then count which products stay as solids.
walkthrough:
**Identify M and Q from carbonate addition**

Both $\text{Mg(NO}_3)_2$ and $\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2$ undergo precipitation with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$. Group 2 carbonates are insoluble.

$$\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + \text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCO}_3(s)$$
$$\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaCO}_3(s)$$ 
So M is $\text{MgCO}_3$ and Q is $\text{BaCO}_3$, both white precipitates. That is 2 so far.

**Add excess HCl to get N and R**

Carbonates dissolve in excess dilute acid to give soluble chlorides plus $\text{CO}_2$ and water. All chlorides of Group 2 are soluble.

$$\text{MgCO}_3(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2(aq) + \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
$$\text{BaCO}_3(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaCl}_2(aq) + \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$ 
So N is $\text{MgCl}_2(aq)$ and R is $\text{BaCl}_2(aq)$. Neither is a precipitate.

**Add excess NaOH to get P and S**

Now think about Group 2 hydroxides. Solubility increases down the group. Magnesium hydroxide is insoluble, barium hydroxide is soluble.

$$\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2(s)$$
$$\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{Ba(OH)}_2(aq)$$ 
So P is $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, a white precipitate. S is $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$, which stays in solution, so no precipitate.

**Count the white precipitates**

M is precipitate, N is solution, P is precipitate. Q is precipitate, R is solution, S is solution.

That gives M, P and Q only, a total of 3 white precipitates.

options.A: 2 is too low. It usually comes from counting only M and Q as carbonates and forgetting that $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is also insoluble and gives a white precipitate for P.
options.B: 3 is correct. M ($\text{MgCO}_3$), Q ($\text{BaCO}_3$) and P ($\text{Mg(OH)}_2$) are white precipitates, while N ($\text{MgCl}_2$), R ($\text{BaCl}_2$) and S ($\text{Ba(OH)}_2$) are soluble and stay in solution.
options.C: 4 is wrong. It often comes from thinking S is a precipitate like P. In fact solubility of hydroxides increases down Group 2, so $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is soluble while $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is insoluble.
options.D: 5 is wrong. It comes from assuming chlorides N and R or hydroxide S also precipitate. All Group 2 chlorides are soluble, and barium hydroxide is soluble, so only the two carbonates and magnesium hydroxide precipitate.
